questions.question: State Hückel's rule and use it to classify benzene (6 π electrons) and cyclooctatetraene (8 π electrons).
questions.solution: A planar, cyclic, fully conjugated system with (4n + 2) π electrons is aromatic. Benzene: 6 = 4(1)+2 → aromatic. Cyclooctatetraene: 8 = 4(2), which fits 4n, not 4n+2 — it is NOT aromatic; it avoids the instability by puckering out of planarity. All four conditions (planar, cyclic, conjugated, 4n+2) must hold.

questions.question: In Friedel–Crafts alkylation, why is the alkyl halide alone not enough — what does AlCl₃ do?
questions.solution: AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid: it coordinates the halide, polarising R–X to generate the electrophile R⁺ (or a strongly polarised complex) that the benzene ring can attack. Without the catalyst there is no sufficiently strong electrophile — benzene's stable π system ignores weak ones. The catalyst manufactures the attacking species.

questions.question: Why does –CH₃ direct incoming electrophiles to ortho/para while –NO₂ directs to meta?
questions.solution: Both effects act through the stability of the arenium (σ-complex) intermediate. –CH₃ donates (+I/hyperconjugation), stabilising the σ-complex most when attack is o/p (positive charge can sit next to the methyl). –NO₂ withdraws (−I, −M), destabilising the σ-complex most at o/p — meta attack avoids placing positive charge beside the NO₂, so it is the least-bad route. Rate: CH₃ activates, NO₂ deactivates.

questions.question: Why is toluene more reactive than benzene toward nitration?
questions.solution: The methyl group donates electron density into the ring (+I, hyperconjugation), raising the ring's π electron density — the electrophile NO₂⁺ finds an easier target, and the σ-complex is stabilised. Activating substituents lower the rate-determining step's barrier. Electron-rich rings react faster with electrophiles.

questions.question: Why does hot KMnO₄ oxidise toluene all the way to benzoic acid regardless of the side-chain length?
questions.solution: The benzylic C–H bonds (on the carbon attached to the ring) are unusually weak — the resulting benzylic radical/cation is resonance-stabilised by the ring. KMnO₄ abstracts these hydrogens and oxidises the side chain stepwise until only the ring-attached carboxyl remains. Whatever the chain length, oxidation stops at the ring: –COOH.

questions.question: Benzene has three formal double bonds but does not decolourise bromine water. Why not?
questions.solution: Benzene's six pi electrons are delocalised over the ring, not confined to three isolated double bonds. Breaking that aromatic system would cost the large resonance stabilisation energy, so addition is energetically unfavourable. Electrophilic SUBSTITUTION preserves aromaticity by replacing a hydrogen instead. Aromatic stability, not lack of unsaturation, blocks addition.

questions.concept: Why benzene has exactly six pi electrons
questions.question: Cyclooctatetraene has alternating double bonds too, yet is non-aromatic. Give the criteria that benzene meets and this compound fails.
questions.solution: Hückel's rule requires a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated system with 4n+2 pi electrons. Benzene: planar, cyclic, conjugated, 6 electrons (n = 1) → aromatic. Cyclooctatetraene has 8 pi electrons (4n, not 4n+2) and puckers out of planarity to escape antiaromaticity → non-aromatic. Aromaticity is a numeric and geometric condition, not simply the presence of alternating bonds.

questions.question: Benzene reacts with bromine only in the presence of FeBr₃, yet bromine is already electrophilic. Why is a catalyst necessary?
questions.solution: Molecular Br₂ is not electrophilic enough to attack the stable aromatic ring. FeBr₃ polarises Br–Br to create a much stronger electrophile (Br⁺-like, complexed), enough to break aromaticity in the intermediate. The catalyst activates the reagent, not the substrate, and is regenerated at the end.
